post.caption: Some diamonds glow blue under UV light. Roughly 25 to 35 percent of gem diamonds fluoresce to some degree, and more than 95 percent of those glow blue under UV light. A gap surrounded by three nitrogen atoms usually causes the blue glow. In 1663, Robert Boyle reported a diamond that shone in the dark, and George Stokes coined the word fluorescence in 1852. He took the name from fluorspar, a mineral that also glows. GIA reports it from none to very strong. Daylight includes long-wave UV, the light that sets off the blue glow. In daylight, blue fluorescence can make a yellowish diamond look whiter.
